comparator.name: Applied Mathematics
comparator.sourceNotes: The 2026–2027 regulations prescribe a 165 EC major and 15 EC minor in the standard route. This example uses the Applied Mathematics first-year project, the first two listed choices in each upper-year group and Statistical Modelling as the remaining elective.

components.name: First-year Project Applied Mathematics
components.note: The Applied Mathematics project is one of two first-year choices. Students draw on first-year mathematics to investigate an applied problem.

components.name: Differential Equations in Science and Engineering
Project Mathematical Modelling
components.note: One of the two required modelling or systems project choices illustrated here. Uses earlier differential equations, numerical methods and scientific computing.

components.name: Project Systems Theory
components.note: The second project choice illustrated here. Builds on first-year Linear Systems.

components.name: Numerical Linear Algebra
components.note: One of two advanced choices illustrated here. Uses earlier linear algebra and numerical analysis, including Python.

components.name: Advanced Systems Theory
components.note: The other advanced choice illustrated here. Builds on Linear Algebra 1 and 2 and Linear Systems.

components.name: Mathematics & Society: Ethical and Professional Aspects
Statistical Modelling
components.note: The example uses Statistical Modelling as the elective. It builds on Probability Theory and Statistics.

components.name: Preparation Bachelor's Project
components.note: Builds on the first-year project and second-year mathematics and must be completed before the bachelor’s project.

components.name: Bachelor's Project Applied Mathematics
components.note: Requires completion of year one and 150 EC in the degree, including project preparation, with an approved study programme and career portfolio. Students must also enrol in the project.

components.name: Minor
components.note: The standard route includes 15 EC of minor space. The courses depend on the minor chosen.

alternativeSelection.assessment: Three distinct options share a quantitative foundation. The closest option focuses on mathematical and computational models of autonomous systems. The other options apply quantitative methods to Earth and energy systems or to bioscience and health.

comparisonAlignment.rationale: Both use programming to solve problems. Groningen builds directly on calculus and linear algebra in scientific programming.
Both use logic, sets and proof. Groningen continues this foundation into proof-based analysis.
Both introduce differentiation and integration. UCR also uses complex numbers and differential equations in a dynamic modelling project.
Both address optimisation; UCR focuses on search and constraint-satisfaction methods for AI rather than a full applied-mathematics optimisation course.
Both directly study systems of equations, vectors, matrices and linear spaces; Groningen continues to a second dedicated linear-algebra course.
Both study numerical integration, interpolation and equation solving. UCR tests accuracy and stability using Mathematica, while Groningen uses Python.
Both use differential equations to analyse linear systems. UCR emphasizes signals, transforms and feedback. Groningen continues into advanced systems theory.
Both establish probability concepts and distributions; UCR combines probability with statistical inference and simulation.
Both develop statistical models; UCR teaches regression, classification and machine-learning methods rather than Groningen's dedicated Statistical Modelling elective.
Both extend calculus to several variables. UCR also introduces complex-valued functions and differential equations.

notes.text: The UCR options share methods in calculus, numerical computing, linear systems and modelling. Groningen requires a deeper sequence in proof-based analysis, topology, differential equations and systems theory, along with staged mathematical projects and a dedicated bachelor’s project.

audience.programmeDescription: Applied Mathematics at the University of Groningen combines mathematical proof with modelling and computation. Students develop methods for analysing systems, solve problems from science and engineering, and complete an applied mathematics research project.
audience.comparisonExplanation: UCR offers related study in mathematical modelling and autonomous systems, Earth and energy systems, or quantitative bioscience. Groningen develops greater depth in mathematical proof, analysis, differential equations and systems theory.
